query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: For high-temperature wear applications, the overall wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating is primarily governed by the formation of a copper‐rich, protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure. This oxide layer, resulting from thermally activated copper segregation and subsequent oxidation, acts as a lubricious barrier that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during wear.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating, as-deposited with a homogenous microstructure on a conventional metal substrate
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-oxidation treatment at elevated temperature (e.g., 800 °C for a fixed duration) to promote the formation of the copper-enriched surface oxide, compared to keeping the coating at room temperature prior to wear testing
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted at a high-temperature regime (approximately 600–800 °C) under controlled sliding loads that simulate harsh operational environments
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a copper-rich oxide scale at the coating surface, possibly accompanied by local phase segregation
generation.mechanism: High-temperature exposure causes copper to segregate and oxidize preferentially, forming a dense, lubricious oxide layer. This layer reduces friction and abrasive wear by acting as a barrier between the sliding surface and the bulk coating, thereby protecting the underlying material against oxidation and mechanical degradation
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, pre-oxidized coatings should exhibit a significantly reduced wear rate and lower friction during high-temperature sliding wear tests compared to the as-deposited (unoxidized) baseline coatings. Microstructural analysis should reveal a continuous, copper-enriched oxide scale on the pre-treated samples.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating without high-temperature pre-oxidation treatment (as-deposited state), tested under the same high-temperature wear conditions
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be observable within the 600–800 °C range under typical mechanical loading conditions for high-temperature applications. At temperatures significantly higher or under extreme mechanical loads, the integrity of the oxide layer may be compromised, altering wear behavior
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of copper segregation and oxide scale formation, as well as the potential impact on coating adhesion, remain uncertain until quantified by detailed microstructural and wear studies

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on conventional metal substrates. Subject one set to a controlled high-temperature pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., 800 °C for 2 hours) to encourage the formation of the copper-rich oxide scale and leave the other set in the as-deposited state. Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests (within the 600–800 °C range) under identical mechanical loading and duration. Post-test, perform detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM, EDS, and XRD) to assess the presence and integrity of the oxide layer.
measurements: Wear rate (using mass loss or volume loss measurements)
Coefficient of friction during wear tests
Surface oxide composition and thickness (via EDS and XRD)
Adhesion quality of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction compared to the as-deposited baseline, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal the formation of a continuous, copper-enriched oxide layer on the treated samples, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. The average hardness of the WVTaTiCr alloy coating reaches 627.36 HV. After 50 h of high-temperature oxidation, the oxide weight of WVTaTiCr increases by 5.12 m
The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures.

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
